project.name: opensourcedating
project.name_note: Working title. No name has been chosen yet.
project.tagline: An open-source dating app, piloted in Berlin. You search and read profiles instead of swiping, write one thoughtful opening message, and chat end-to-end encrypted.
project.stage_detail: Writing the spec. No app code yet; the first test will use fake data only.
project.note: Decided means Hendrik decided it. Planned means agreed as a later step but not designed yet. Guess means a working assumption or a recommendation still waiting for a decision. Open means nobody has decided yet.

intro.what: A free, open-source dating app for Android and iOS. It starts as a pilot in Berlin on one server run by a small non-profit, and later grows into a network of vetted servers run by different operators, so no single company owns the people who use it.

why.title: Dating apps are built to keep you swiping
why.text: Card stacks, endless feeds and hidden ranking reward quick judgements on a photo and time spent in the app, not good conversations.

why.title: Visibility is for sale
why.text: Boosts, paid likes and premium tiers decide who gets seen. We don't sell visibility at all.

why.title: The data is about as sensitive as data gets
why.text: Sexuality, gender, location and private chats. Leaks and data sales have hurt real people, queer users most of all. We treat all of it as special-category data under GDPR.

why.title: Nobody can check what the apps do
why.text: The big apps are closed. Ours is public code anyone can read, test and run, with no patents.

principles.title: Search, don't swipe
principles.text: Filter and browse a results list, like old OkCupid. Read profiles, compare, come back later. No card stack, no endless feed.

principles.title: One opening message
principles.text: Anyone can write one text-only message to anyone they can see, with a small weekly allowance. A reply starts the conversation; silence is a normal no.

principles.title: Chats only the two of you can read
principles.text: End-to-end encrypted with libsignal (the Signal protocol). The server passes messages on and deletes them once delivered.

principles.title: Location you choose
principles.text: No GPS. You pick a home area on a Berlin map at the precision you want. Others see travel time by public transport, never a distance.

principles.title: No hidden ranking, nothing for sale
principles.text: You choose the sort order. No paid boosts, no "who viewed me", no "online now".

principles.title: Safety built in from day one
principles.text: Hide, block and report (reporting always blocks), a separate safety service, verifiable reports and an 18+ check that stores only the result.

principles.title: Open source, run by a non-profit
principles.text: Public repo, no patents. A Berlin non-profit association runs the pilot server before real users join.

principles.title: Test data until it's reviewed
principles.text: The first pilot uses fake profiles and labelled test bots. Real users only after a human security review and a data protection assessment.

journey.title: Sign up without a password
journey.text: A passkey or a one-time email code (Ory Kratos). No password and no phone number. You confirm you are 18 or older. Your account gets a random ID; your email is never shown or used as a key.

journey.title: Write your profile
journey.text: Long-form texts come first, photos second. Every photo is checked before anyone sees it. How gender, orientation and "looking for" are entered is being designed, with care for the queer community.

journey.title: Pick your home area
journey.text: Tap your area on a Berlin map with a 500 m grid and choose how precisely it is stored. Only that area is kept, never a history. You can move it at most once a day and four times a month, so nobody can use it to pin you down.

journey.title: Search and browse
journey.text: Set filters (travel time, age, gender and "looking for", relationship type, recently active) and browse 20 results a page. Gender is two-way: you only see people who are also looking for someone like you.

journey.title: Write one opening message
journey.text: Text only, no links. You get 5 a week (fewer for new accounts), so you choose carefully. Unanswered messages disappear after 30 days, with no read receipts.

journey.title: A reply starts the conversation
journey.text: From then on you chat end-to-end encrypted. The server only ever holds encrypted messages, and only until they arrive. Either of you can end the conversation at any time.

journey.title: Stay safe
journey.text: Hide someone from your results, block them (silent, both ways) or report them (which always blocks too). Moderators can verify reported messages without the server ever reading chats.

not_building: Swiping, card stacks or one-at-a-time decisions
An endless feed (results are paginated and the list ends)
Photos, links or read receipts in opening messages

mockups.title: Search
mockups.note: The design doc leaves list vs. grid open, and specifies a non-empty state for the early pilot -- shown as three options.

mockups.title: Write & save
mockups.note: One opening message per profile, a reply starts the conversation, and a private Save list nobody is told about.

mockups.title: Chat
mockups.note: A conversation opens once the recipient replies to an opening message; the safety-controls layout isn't designed yet.

mockups.title: Profile
mockups.note: Three profile views (yours, theirs, and the preview card in results), none final. Actions on someone else's profile are Write, Save, Hide, Block and Report.

architecture.summary: Two stages. The Berlin pilot runs on one server operated by an accountable legal entity, because search, blocking, bans and moderation need someone who can enforce rules and act as the GDPR controller. Later, servers run by vetted operators form one decentralised network: no server owns a person, and no server holds a full profile. Stage 1 is built so stage 2 needs no rewrite.

stages.title: Stage 1: one server (Berlin pilot)
stages.summary: Phones talk to a single open-source server in Germany. It handles sign-in, profiles, search by home area, opening-message allowances and the chat relay. Bans, reports and verification live in a separate safety service. Chats are end-to-end encrypted; the relay deletes each message once it is delivered.

stages.title: Stage 2: a network of vetted servers (later)
stages.summary: Other cities or communities run servers that join through an allow-list and a shared safety policy. There are no home servers: nobody belongs to one server. Each person's data (search card, message mailbox, counters) is held by a small group of servers the network picks, and photos and profile texts are encrypted and split into pieces across servers, so no server holds a full profile and some can go offline without losing anything. Servers mainly broker contact: answering searches, passing on messages, and sharing one ban list. How exactly this works is still open.

groundwork: Account IDs that don't depend on any one server (the exact format is being reconsidered, see Open questions).
Safety data (bans, reports, verification) lives in its own service with an API, ready to be shared.
Profile and photo storage sit behind one interface, so sharded storage can replace it later.
Search reads only the fields it needs through its own interface, never the full profile.
Every chat message carries a franking tag, so reports stay verifiable across servers.

decisions.why: Search, blocking and moderation need an accountable operator; one shared pool helps the small pilot.
decisions.alternatives: Federation from day one, pure phone-to-phone

decisions.choice: React Native + Expo, libsignal in our own native Kotlin/Swift module
decisions.why: Fastest for one developer on both platforms; every option needs a native libsignal bridge anyway, and that module is reusable and fundable.
decisions.alternatives: Flutter, Kotlin Multiplatform, fully native Kotlin + Swift

decisions.choice: Ory Kratos with passkeys + email codes
decisions.why: No passwords and no custom auth code to get wrong. How sign-in works without home servers in stage 2 is open.

decisions.choice: Reopened: random ID plus server name (id@server) ties people to a home server. Proposal: an ID made from a key created on the phone. One phone per account and no chat backup stay decided.
decisions.why: The network should have no home servers, and changing IDs later touches every table.

decisions.choice: libsignal end-to-end encryption, opening messages included; relay deletes after delivery
decisions.why: Nothing readable or lasting on the server; works when the other phone is offline.
decisions.alternatives: Matrix (keeps history on servers), pure phone-to-phone (no offline delivery, leaks IPs)

decisions.choice: Bans, reports, verification and photo hashes in a separate service with its own database and API
decisions.why: Lets stage 2 share one ban list between servers without a rewrite.

decisions.choice: Message franking in the message format from v1
decisions.why: Moderators can check reported messages are genuine without the server reading chats.

decisions.choice: Self-chosen home area on a ~500 m grid, stored only at the chosen precision, changes rate-limited
decisions.why: Coarse by default, chosen by the user, hard to triangulate.

decisions.choice: Filtered search, no swiping, user-chosen sort
decisions.why: Better decisions, no dark patterns, no swipe-patent exposure.

decisions.choice: Self-declared for the fake-data test; on-phone selfie estimate plus stronger check near 18 before real users; only the result stored
decisions.why: No ID scans or face data on the server; the method can change behind one interface.

decisions.choice: Own small Hetzner server in Germany, separate from anything else
decisions.why: Cheap, EU-hosted, isolated from other services. Set up and locked down; nothing deployed yet.

decisions.choice: Berlin e.V. (non-profit association), founded before real users join
decisions.why: Someone has to be the GDPR controller and DSA hosting provider.

decisions.choice: Decentralised network of vetted servers: no home servers, an allow-list, one shared safety policy and ban list
decisions.why: No server owns a person; in an open network a banned person would move to the laxest server.
decisions.alternatives: Open federation like Mastodon, pure phone-to-phone

decisions.choice: Encrypted profile pieces spread redundantly across servers; no server holds a full profile
decisions.why: A breach or a rogue operator of one server can't read whole profiles, and profiles survive servers going offline.
decisions.alternatives: Each server keeps its own users' full profiles

decisions.choice: Proposal: a small group of servers picked by the network from the account ID, acting only when most of the group agrees
decisions.why: No single server owns a person, and any one server can fail. Costs: much more engineering, slower search, and Ory Kratos would not fit stage 2.

topics.intro: Every key feature and rule is reviewed one topic at a time before prototype code is written, costliest to change later first. Each decided topic has its own spec file.

items.title: Accounts and identity
points: Passkeys or email codes, no passwords, no phone number.
Reopened: the account ID format. id@server ties a person to a home server; the proposal is an ID made from a key created on the phone. Email is never a key either way.
One phone per account in the pilot, no chat backup. A lost phone gets the account back, but not old chats.

items.title: Gender, orientation and "looking for"
points: Decided: gender filtering is two-way.
Decided: the data model supports the queer community from the first version, even though that community joins later.
A proposal is waiting for Hendrik (see Open questions).

items.title: Who sees what, and when
points: A proposal is waiting for Hendrik: two-way "who can find me" limits, a fit checklist, an inbox cap and five visibility steps (see Open questions).

items.title: Opening messages and conversations
points: One text-only opening message per person, 5 a week to start; a reply starts the conversation.
Opening messages are end-to-end encrypted too; "no links" is enforced on the recipient's phone.
Either person can end a conversation; after that neither can write again, but it isn't a block.

items.title: Safety and moderation
points: Hide, block (silent, both ways) and report (always blocks). Reported people hear only when action is taken, with reasons and appeal.
Separate safety service from day one; verifiable reports through message franking.
Ban evasion via hashed email, photo-file hashes and device signals, never face recognition.

items.title: Location
points: No GPS; a self-chosen home area, stored only at the precision the user picked.
Home area changes at most once a day and four times in 30 days.
Travel-time bands by public transport, never distances.

items.title: Photos and profile storage
points: A proposal is waiting for Hendrik: photos checked before they go public, each encrypted with its own key, and a conversation-only tier (see Open questions).

items.title: Age check (18+)
points: Self-declared date of birth for the fake-data test.
Before real users: on-phone selfie estimate, stronger check near 18, the EU age app once available.
Only the result is stored, never a selfie or an ID.

items.title: Deletion, retention and export
points: Pros and cons are written up and waiting for Hendrik (see Open questions).

items.title: Search limits
points: 20 results a page, and the list ends.
50 full-profile views a day for new accounts, 200 after two weeks, to slow down scrapers.
"Hide" lasts until you undo it.

items.title: Test bots
points: Every bot and its data is flagged and wipeable in one go; testers see a "test bot" badge.
Generated photos only. Bots run on a separate machine through the public API, rate limits on.
Attack bots try to locate users and copy profiles; the tests fail if they succeed.

items.title: Stage 2: network of servers
points: A decentralised network of vetted servers with one shared ban list. No home servers.
No server holds a full profile: encrypted pieces spread redundantly across servers.
Who holds each person's data, how sign-in works, and what search can read are still open.

other.title: Pilot scope
other.text: Berlin, city-wide. Phase 1 is a technical test with the Berlin tech scene using fake data. The queer community joins only once gender, preference and safety features are solid.

other.title: Build our own
other.text: We build a new app rather than fork Alovoa, the existing open-source dating app, and borrow ideas from it.

other.title: Open and unpatented
other.text: Public repository from the start, no patents.

items: How groups of servers agree on counters and signatures (replication method).
Which fields the readable search card holds.
Who holds the keys to profile pieces, and how a viewer gets access.
Splitting method and the values of k and n.
Which protocol servers use to talk to each other.
How deletion reaches every piece, and what the joint-controller agreement contains.
The list of report reasons, response times, and who moderates during the test.
Retention periods for reports, decisions and ban records (lawyer).
Which location precisions are offered and which is the default.
Allowance numbers for new accounts.
Rate limits on search requests.

Who runs and pays for the server before the e.V. exists.

roadmap.title: Research and ground rules
items: Research on GDPR in Berlin, data security, safety and moderation, hostile actors, funding and launch.
Core design: search instead of swiping, one opening message, coarse location, two stages.
App framework chosen; pilot server set up in Germany.

roadmap.title: Spec review
items: 8 of 12 topics decided; 5 proposals waiting for a decision (see Open questions).
Funding applications: NLnet (deadline 3 Nov 2026) and the Prototype Fund (30 Nov 2026).

roadmap.title: Prototype with fake data
items: Server, safety service and the libsignal native module.
Android and iOS app; labelled test bots, including attack bots.
Testers from the Berlin tech scene, using fake profiles only.

roadmap.title: Before any real user
items: Human security review of the server, relay and sign-in.
Found the Berlin e.V. as operator; data protection impact assessment and an external data protection officer.
Stronger age check, in-app data export, lawyer on retention periods.

roadmap.title: Real dating in Berlin
items: Invite-only waves, kept balanced, recruited at events.
The queer community joins once gender, preference and safety features are solid.

roadmap.title: Stage 2: network of servers
items: Other cities or communities run vetted servers in one decentralised network; profiles split across them.

suggestions.intro: Recommendations from the research that still need a decision. Have an idea of your own? Open an issue on GitHub.

items.title: Apply to the Prototype Fund
items.summary: Pays developer time on public-interest open source (up to 47,500 € for one person). Current round closes 30 Nov 2026.

items.title: Apply to NLnet for one component
items.summary: For example the libsignal module for React Native/Expo or the encrypted chat relay. Deadline 3 Nov 2026, noon CET.

items.title: Found a Berlin e.V. before phase 2
items.summary: No entity needed for the fake-data test; the e.V. becomes the operator before real users join, with an asset lock in its statutes.

items.title: Write down why phase 1 needs no DPO
items.summary: Holds only while phase 1 really uses fake data. A DPIA and an external DPO are needed once real dating data comes in.

items.title: Human security review before any real data
items.summary: Keep the pilot on test data until a person has reviewed the server, the relay and the sign-in setup.

items.title: Invite-only waves, balanced and recruited at events
items.summary: Gate waves so the gender and orientation mix stays balanced; open an area only once new users would see real profiles on day one.

items.title: Contact the Alovoa maintainer
items.summary: Report their encryption issue privately through their SECURITY.md and ask about sharing pieces later.

items.title: Register the name as a trademark
items.summary: Once a name is chosen: German mark at the DPMA (around 290 €) before phase 2; consider an EU mark if stage 2 reaches other countries.
